newsitem.title: TURKEY: U.S. firm KMR Power plans investments in Turkey. [CORRECTED 17:12 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. firm KMR Power plans investments in Turkey. [CORRECTED 17:12 GMT]

text.p: Independent U.S. power company KMR (corrects from KMW) Power Corp is planning to invest in power projects in energy-hungry Turkey, where power demand rises at an annual rate of 11 percent, the company president said.
"We are committed to Turkey for a long term," said George Kappaz on the sidelines of an energy meeting in Ankara.
"Turkey is one of the top three countries we are interested in. It has a all the ingredients of the emerging giants," he told Reuters.

KMR Power, an Arlington, Virgina-based private firm, is leading a consortium which includes the U.S. Stone and Webster and Turkish Merka in its bid for a $500 million, 700-MegaWatt (MW) gas-fired power plant in Adapazari, to the east of Istanbul.

The constortium contends with eight other international consortia in the tender, which the energy ministry has been evaluating since it collected bids for six thermal power plants including Adapazari on February 28.
He said he believed the Turkish energy ministry would go ahead with its multi-billion dollar power projects despite legal challenges by the country's top courts.
"Turkey needs power for a strong economy. It will eliminate all those obstacles. And we are committed regardless of what has happened," he said.
The government has prepared a law to overcome the legal snags to the build-operate-transfer and build-operate models for big infrastructure projects.
The ministry will announce the results of the tenders after the law is passed in parliament, which officials said would be in late April.
Kappaz said KMR planned other investments in Turkey, which has a power shortage of 2.5 billion kilowatt-hours this year and has begun electricity imports from Iran, Bulgaria and Georgia.
"Turkey needs to invest $3 to $4 billion every year for power plant projects. So there is a big potential for investment here," he said.
He said the consortium had an "excellent" chance of winning the Adapazari tender.
"I think we are the only company which bid with a line of credit for the project," he said.

He said the company had secured a $500-million "non-recourse facility" from Chase Manhattan to be partly used in the financing of the plant. "If we win the tender, we are ready to begin the construction within one year from the award," he said.
The consortium will seek another Turkish contractor partner if it wins the tender, he said.
